topic: Compile-Time Polymorphism vs Runtime Virtual Functions
explanation: This explores how C++ templates, particularly template metaprogramming, enable compile-time polymorphism.  This differs significantly from runtime polymorphism achieved with virtual functions.  Compile-time polymorphism leverages the compiler to generate specialized code for different template arguments at compile time, avoiding runtime overhead associated with virtual function calls.  The compiler's behavior involves generating distinct functions or data structures for each template instantiation, leading to potential code bloat if many instantiations exist.  Understanding the compiler's template instantiation process—including recursive template instantiations—is crucial for performance tuning and avoiding unexpected behavior.  Memory layout depends entirely on the types used in the instantiation; no common base class exists to dictate layout as in runtime polymorphism. Assembly-level analysis would reveal distinct function bodies generated for different types.  We'll examine the trade-offs between compile-time versus runtime overhead, focusing on performance implications of increased code size and the potential for faster execution due to the absence of virtual function calls.
